alignment.note: The Greek ἦλθον and Latin venerunt are third-person plural ('they came'), reflecting Jesus and the disciples; the Peshitta ܘܐܬܐ is singular ('and he came'), focusing on Jesus alone. The Syriac verb is fused with the conjunction, hence its index recurs in both the conjunction and verb groups.

Greek uses the substantivised adverb τὸ πέραν ('the other side') as the object of εἰς; the Vulgate renders this with the preposition trans plus fretum ('across the strait'), making the crossing explicit; the Syriac ܠܥܒܪܐ (from root ʿ-b-r, 'to cross over') compactly expresses the same notion of the opposite shore in a single prepositional noun.

Greek θαλάσσης and Syriac ܕܝܡܐ denote 'sea' (i.e. the Sea of Galilee), while the Vulgate maris is governed by fretum, characterising the body of water as a strait; the difference is one of geographic register rather than reference.
χώραν / ܠܐܬܪܐ / regionem — all denote 'the region'.

The toponym shows the well-known textual variation: Greek transmits Γερασηνῶν (with the variant Γεργεσηνῶν noted in the lemma) and Latin Gerasenorum, while the Syriac ܕܓܕܪܝܐ reflects the 'Gadarenes' reading (cf. Matt 8:28), a divergence among the manuscript traditions over the precise locality east of the lake.
